chapters.title: Why it really ended (your side of it)
chapters.teaser: Not who was right. What your soul was doing while it fell apart.

chapters.title: Your breakup pattern
chapters.teaser: How you end things, how you grieve, and the habit that slows you down.

chapters.title: Why you keep checking
chapters.teaser: What the pull back toward them is really asking for.

chapters.title: So, will they come back? The honest answer
chapters.teaser: What a chart can and can't tell you, and the question that matters more.

chapters.title: If they ever reach out
chapters.teaser: Three questions to ask before you reply, built for your soul.

chapters.title: What you do now
chapters.teaser: The next small steps that help, whatever they decide.

text.why-it-ended: Gap Wood grows straight up, and that's both the gift and the problem. In your last relationship you probably knew where you were going, and you assumed they were coming with you. When things got hard, you didn't bend. You explained, you planned, you fixed. What you may not have done is ask what they needed and then actually wait for the answer. A breakup with a tall tree is rarely about one fight. It's about a slow feeling, on their side or yours, of living inside someone else's plan. That isn't a crime. It's a habit, and habits can be seen. Name it honestly and you already hold more of this story than you think.
text.your-breakup-pattern: Here's how you tend to end things: late. Gap Wood stays because leaving feels like failing, and you don't fail, you persevere. So you hold on past the point where holding helps, and then one day you're simply done, and the door closes with a sound nobody expected. Afterward you go quiet and productive. New gym routine, new project, maybe a new haircut. It looks like healing. Sometimes it's pride wearing running shoes. The pattern to watch is treating grief like a task with a deadline. Grief doesn't take orders. Let it be slow for a while. You're allowed to be a tree in winter.
text.the-pull: So why do you keep thinking about them? For you it's rarely loneliness. It's the unfinished argument. Gap Wood wants to be understood, and a breakup leaves the case open. You replay conversations and write better answers in the shower. You want them to finally see what you meant. That pull is real, but notice what it's asking for: not them, exactly, but closure on your terms. You can give yourself a lot of that. Write the final speech. Say it out loud to your ceiling. Then ask whether you still want the person, or just the last word.
text.the-honest-answer: Will they come back? Nobody can read that from your birth date, and anyone who says they can is selling something. Their choices belong to them. What your chart can show is what you'd be walking back into. For Gap Wood the real question is this: would you return as the same tree? If it ended because you led and they felt unheard, a reunion without change just replays the same season. If you'd want them back, the honest work is growing a branch you didn't have before. Patience. Curiosity. The ability to lose an argument gracefully. That's useful whether they ever call or not.
text.if-they-reach-out: If a message ever arrives, your instinct will be to answer fast and steer. Don't. Gap Wood decides with the head and calls it the heart. Give yourself a full day. Then ask three things. Has anything actually changed, on either side, or are we just bored? Can I hear their version without correcting it? Would I choose this person if I met them fresh today? If the answers are yes, talk slowly, ideally in person. If they're shaky, a kind short reply is a complete reply. You don't owe anyone a reunion just because they knocked.
text.what-you-do-now: Grow sideways for a while. You've been growing up, toward goals and plans. Now spend some energy on width: friends you neglected, a hobby with no finish line, one thing you're bad at and enjoy anyway. Gap Wood heals through being useful, so let yourself help someone, but don't hide in it. Sleep. Eat real food. Delete the drafts folder if it's getting long. And notice who you are when nobody needs you to lead. That person is the one your next relationship, with them or with someone new, actually gets to meet.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You loved hard and planned a whole future. That's not a flaw, Gap.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Sure. You just forgot to ask if they wanted the same future.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Missing them doesn't mean leaving was wrong.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: And replaying the fight in the shower doesn't count as closure.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Grow a new branch. Patience looks good on you.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Their next move is theirs. Yours is yours. Focus on yours.

spring.intro: Born in spring, Gap Wood, you arrived when every tree was shooting upward at once. Wood was in command of the season, so your chart got a double dose of yourself: tall, certain, rooted. In a breakup that means you probably decided early what the story was and have defended it ever since. You were right about some of it. The spring tree's problem is that it grows toward the light without checking what it shaded on the way. If they said you never bent, they may have had a point. The good news comes from the same place: a spring tree regrows fast. Your recovery starts properly once you stop arguing the case in your head.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You won that argument in your head four hundred times. Feel better yet?

summer.intro: Summer-born Gap Wood grows in heat. Fire ruled your birth month, and a tree's whole job in summer is to feed that fire, so your chart pours energy outward: plans, effort, big gestures, words. In love you probably gave a lot and said a lot. Maybe too much of both in the final months, when the gestures got louder because the connection felt quieter. A summer tree can scorch itself and call it devotion. The breakup may have left you less heartbroken than burnt out, and those two feel identical at 2am. Water is your relief: rest, quiet, people who ask nothing of you. Let yourself be watered before you decide what any of it meant.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You gave so much it singed you a little. Rest first, decide later.

autumn.intro: Autumn is the axe season for a tree. Metal was in command when you were born, Gap Wood, and Metal cuts Wood. That's why you carry a stern inner judge. You hold yourself to rules, and after a breakup you likely turned that blade inward: a list of every mistake, reviewed nightly. Autumn trees also learn to drop their leaves and survive, which is the gift buried in this chart. You can let something go cleanly once you've truly decided it's done. The danger is deciding too fast, out of pride, and then quietly checking their profile for months to make sure you were right. Pruning is meant to help growth. Make sure you're pruning, not punishing.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your inner judge has held court every night this month. Adjourn, please.

winter.intro: A winter tree looks bare, but its roots are drinking. Water rules winter, and Water feeds Wood, so your chart is well supported underneath even when it looks still on top. In a breakup you probably went quiet. Fewer posts, fewer words, a lot of thinking. People may assume you're fine, or cold. You're neither. You're absorbing. The risk for winter Wood is that all that nourishment turns into overthinking: you keep feeding the memory instead of the next season. Rereading old messages counts as watering the past. You have more in reserve than you feel right now. The spring in you is real. It just needs warmth, daylight and other people to start moving.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You look still, Gap. Underneath, your roots are busy healing you.

strength.strong: Your chart backs you up, Gap Wood. Plenty of Wood and Water around your Day Master means you stand tall and rarely doubt your read on things. In a breakup that strength shows up as certainty: you know what went wrong, and it mostly involves them. Some of that may be fair. The blind spot is that a strong tree blocks light without noticing. Your ex may have felt overruled more than unloved. If you're tempted to reach out, check whether you want connection or a rematch. Bending one branch does not make you a smaller tree.
strength.weak: Your chart gives your Day Master little backup, Gap. A tree without much Water or Wood around it grows with effort, and in love you may have tried to earn your place by being useful, agreeable and always available. When it ended, you probably blamed yourself first and loudest. That habit isn't honesty. It's a thirsty root. You weren't too much, and you weren't too little either. Before wondering about them, rebuild your own supports: friends who know you well, routines that steady you, small wins that remind you how you grow.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and answers, even in heartbreak. You want a plan for getting over it, maybe even a plan for getting them back. Slow down. Not everything grows on schedule, and some things need to just sit for a while. Ask for help instead of turning healing into a project. For balance, let a little Metal in: declutter, finish old things, clear out the drafts folder. A clean edge helps Wood stop reaching for what's already gone.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means fresh starts feel heavy. After a breakup you might stay in the same place, emotionally and literally, for longer than you'd like. That isn't weakness. It just means new growth needs a nudge. Small steps work best: a new route to work, one new class, one new person a week. Get outside in the mornings and keep something green near you. You don't need a whole new life. You need one new branch, and then another.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire makes you feel everything at full volume. A breakup can feel like an emergency, with urges to text, post, or fix it all tonight. Your passion is real, but heat isn't a strategy. Before any big move, sleep on it. Cool down with water: swimming, long showers, quiet evenings at home. Talk to your calmest friend before your most exciting one. Let the fire warm you instead of burning through your peace.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means joy and visibility don't come easily, and after a breakup you might go dim for a while, hiding from people and from fun. Turn the lights back on gently. Sunshine, music, dancing in the kitchen, one social plan a week even when you'd rather stay in. Letting people see you is the medicine here. Warmth doesn't only live in romance. It's in friends, in laughter, in simply being out in the world.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you hold on: to routines, to memories, to the hope that things will settle back into their old place. Stability is your gift, but in heartbreak it can turn into staying stuck. Shake the ground a little. Move the furniture, take a short trip, try something unplanned. Let some Wood energy in, growth and new beginnings. You can keep what was good and still leave room for something new to grow.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means life can feel unsteady, and a breakup can knock away what little ground you had. You might feel scattered, unsure where to put your feet. Build structure gently: regular meals, a steady bedtime, one place at home that's only yours. Cook something. Walk somewhere. Lean on the people who are reliable. Stability first, big decisions later. You need solid ground under you before deciding anything about the past.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal makes you sharp and decisive, sometimes too quickly. You may have cut the relationship off cleanly and then refused to look at what you feel. Or you judge yourself harshly for every mistake you made in it. Soften the edges. Let Water in: rest, tears, music, journaling. Feeling the grief isn't the same as reopening the door. You can keep your boundaries firm and still let your heart thaw.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard, so after a breakup you might keep the door half open, answer every message, or stay friends when it hurts. Practise clean edges. Mute without guilt. Box up their things. Say no without explaining. White and silver, tidy spaces and finished tasks all help your chart. A boundary isn't cold. It's how you protect the part of you that's still healing.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means you think and feel deeply, maybe endlessly. After a breakup you might drift through memories, analyse every detail, and lose sleep to what-ifs. Your intuition is a gift, but it needs riverbanks. Add some Earth: routines, cooking, walks, people who ground you. Give overthinking a time limit. Feel it fully, then get up and do one ordinary thing.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means rest and reflection get skipped. You may rush past the breakup, staying busy so you never have to sit with it. That works until suddenly it doesn't. Build in quiet on purpose: slow mornings, water by your bed, a few lines in a journal at night, a bath instead of another plan. Let yourself feel without fixing. Intuition grows when you give it some silence.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: So much Wood. You've drafted three versions of 'hey, random but' already.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy wants a goal. Give it your own plans, not their inbox.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: every feeling is a five-alarm emergency. It's a breakup, not an inferno.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is beautiful. Let it cool before you hit send on anything.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth. You'd still be in that relationship purely out of habit.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your loyalty is rare. Just make sure you're loyal to yourself too.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal. You cut them off cleanly, then reread everything at midnight.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Being firm protected you. Being gentle with yourself will heal you.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you've cried to three songs and written a novel in your notes app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Feeling deeply is a gift. Just come up for air sometimes.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make moving on feel stuck. Small new routines count as growth.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: You haven't changed anything since the breakup, including your lock screen. Start there.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make joy feel far away. Borrow some from a loud friend.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: You stopped having fun when they left. Fun was never theirs to take.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth can make everything feel unsteady. Simple routines will hold you.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no anchor. You re-decide whether to text them every hour.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal makes boundaries tricky. You're allowed to say no to your own phone.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means you'll answer at 2am. Put the phone in another room.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make grief hide. It's okay to let it surface slowly.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: You said you're fine twelve times today. Water would like a word.

gap-wood.title: Two trees, one standoff
gap-wood.text: You dated your own reflection, and for a while that felt like finally being understood. Two Gap Woods talk about values on the second date and five-year plans by the fifth. Nobody played games. Plans were confirmed, links were sent, dinner was booked by Tuesday. Then came the first real disagreement, and neither of you bent. Not loudly. Just a long, polite silence where both of you waited for the other to say sorry first, because both of you were quietly certain you were right. That's the particular ache here: it didn't end with a bang, it ended with two people standing very straight in separate rooms. What pulls you back is respect. You rarely meet someone with a spine like that, and you miss being taken seriously by an equal. You also miss winning the argument, if we're being honest. Here's what's in your hands. Write down the fight as they would tell it, in their words, as generously as you can manage. If you can do that without adding a rebuttal at the bottom, you've grown a branch that relationship never had. Whatever you decide next, take that branch with you.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You found someone as principled as you. That's rare, and it's okay to miss it.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: You also found someone as stubborn as you. Who apologised first? Exactly. Nobody.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Being right gets lonely when it's the only thing you kept.

eul-wood.title: The tree and the vine that let go
eul-wood.text: Your Eul Wood ex wound into your life so easily that you barely noticed how much of it they were holding up. The voice notes. The apartment links you couldn't afford. The sticker at 11pm that really meant 'are we okay?' And you, being a tree, replied 'ok' and went to sleep, because to you 'ok' meant ok. To them it read like a closed door. Over time you felt like a support beam, and they felt like they were climbing something that never leaned toward them. They agreed with you to your face and then did it their own way, and you called that sneaky. They might have called it survival. The hurt here is quiet: you didn't lose a fight, you lost a texture. Your phone is so tidy now, and you hate it a little. What pulls you back is that softness. Nobody else made your rigid days feel lighter. Here's something useful: scroll the old chat, not for the sweet bits, but to count how often you asked a question back. That number is the lesson. It isn't a verdict on you. It's simply the next branch to grow.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: 'Ok' was not a love letter, Gap. It wasn't a breakup text either.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Eul, your voice notes were adorable. You were allowed to want more than one sentence back.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Next time, say the thing before the sticker.

byeong-fire.title: Firewood for the sun
byeong-fire.text: You were the firewood. That's the plain version. Your Byeong Fire ex lit up every room, including the one you lived in, and you kept feeding the flame: the late airport pick-ups, the emotional support at 1am, the spontaneous trip you paid half of and planned all of. They didn't mean to take. Suns don't notice the tree getting thinner. They texted in capitals for a week, went quiet for a day, then flooded back with sunset photos as if nothing happened, and you, who prefer steady, started counting the gaps. You never said it out loud. You just grew quieter until one day you were simply done, and they were genuinely shocked, because from where they stood everything was bright. That's why this one hurts strangely: you're grieving someone who was never cruel, and you're angry at yourself for giving past empty. The pull is the warmth. Life with them felt like a long summer. But you can be warm without being burned for fuel. Start by finding out how you feel on a day when nobody needs anything from you. Spend one like that soon. Notice what grows.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Byeong, you gave so much light. You just forgot to check who was holding the match.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, you counted every unanswered text and said nothing. That's not patience, that's a ledger.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Both of you were generous. Neither of you said 'I'm tired.' Start there.

jeong-fire.title: The oak and the March grudge
jeong-fire.text: Your Jeong Fire ex was the candle by the window: quiet, warm, paying attention to everything. They wrote you long messages after midnight and noticed when your reply was two words shorter than usual. You replied like a train timetable. 'Leaving now.' 'Booked.' To you, reliability was the romance. To them, the missing detail was the whole story. Small hurts piled up somewhere you couldn't see, because you assume silence means fine, and then one evening it all burned at once over something you said in March. You defended yourself. You tried to fix their mood with a plan. They didn't want a plan, they wanted you to sit next to the feeling for a minute. So the ending felt to you like a sudden fire, and to them like a slow dimming you never noticed. What keeps tugging is how tender it was. Nobody else has ever remembered your coffee order and your childhood dog's name. The fix is small: practise the one-detail rule now, with friends. Every message gets one line that proves you heard them. It's awkward for a week. Then it's just who you are.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, they weren't psychic. You needed to say it in March, not October.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, one warm detail per text. That's all the candle needed.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two good people, one missing translator.

mu-earth.title: The tree that tried to move a mountain
mu-earth.text: You fell for a mountain and then, being you, tried to improve it. Your Mu Earth ex was steady, unbothered, completely themselves. At first that was restful. Then you started suggesting things: a better job, an earlier alarm, a different way to cook rice. You called it support. They felt managed. Every push you made, they went a little more still, and stillness, to you, looks exactly like rejection. So you pushed harder. They replied when they replied, sometimes hours later, always sincere, and you sat staring at the plan you'd sent at 9am wondering why nobody was answering. That's the shape of this breakup: not a dramatic end, more a slow standoff between growth and staying put, with both of you sure you were the landscape. The pull is how safe they felt. Mountains don't flinch, and you secretly loved that someone could hold you without needing anything fixed. Your homework: notice the urge to manage the people around you this month. A friend's career, your sibling's diet. Catch it, say nothing, and watch what happens. Some people grow better left alone.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Mu, your stillness isn't coldness. Some people just never learned to read it.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, the mountain didn't need a coach. It needed company.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Growth and steadiness can share a landscape. Just not by force.

gi-earth.title: Rooted in the same garden
gi-earth.text: This one was a good match, and that's exactly why it hurts. Your Gi Earth ex was the garden you took root in: the 'did you eat', the 'how did the meeting go', the quiet way your life just worked better with them around. You brought the plans and the direction; they made the ground soft enough to grow in. The pressure point was small and constant. You leaned on them hard and assumed they'd adapt, and they mostly did, without complaining, while privately worrying about everything. You talked, they listened. You shared news; they asked the question. And when they finally said what they'd been carrying, it came out all at once and you felt ambushed by months of silence you never noticed. The pull back is real and specific: you miss being cared for by someone who didn't make it a performance. What you can do starts with a question you probably skipped a hundred times: 'and how was your day?' Ask it of people now and listen to the whole answer. That habit is the soil for anything good you grow next, with anyone.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gi, you were the soil. Soil is allowed to ask for rain.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, 'how was your day' is four words. You had years.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: A strong match still needs both people talking. Keep that lesson close.

gyeong-metal.title: The axe and the oak, over the dishwasher
gyeong-metal.text: You dated an axe. Not a cruel one, an honest one. Your Gyeong Metal ex criticised to improve things: your posture, your plan, the way you load the dishwasher. And you, who have principles about everything, heard every note as an attack on who you are. So you defended. They pushed. Suddenly two people who agreed on almost every big question were at war over cutlery placement, and neither of you was going to apologise first. Your texts were short, theirs were shorter. 'No.' 'Why.' 'Because.' There was respect in it, and warmth too, but nobody said the warm part out loud. You got cut a hundred small times by someone who thought they were helping, and you cut back with sermons they found preachy. What pulls you back is the sparring. Life with them felt sharp and awake, and everyone else seems a bit soft now. Here's a strange experiment: next time someone corrects you, say 'you might be right' before anything else. Just that. Decide later whether they were. It's the oddest freedom a tree can try.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gyeong, I respect the honesty. But 'you're wrong' isn't a love language.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, being corrected isn't being rejected. Breathe before the speech.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two strong people, zero soft sentences. That's the whole post-mortem.

sin-metal.title: The jewel who noticed everything
sin-metal.text: Your Sin Metal ex noticed every flaw and mentioned about a third of them, beautifully phrased, which somehow made it worse. The crease in your shirt. The way you told that story at dinner. Your 'ok 👍' reply to the message they had clearly rewritten three times. You thought effort was just normal, so you never praised it; they wanted their effort seen, every time, specifically. You were blunt in public, which they found mortifying. They were precise in private, which you found exhausting. Two people trying to be good to each other in completely different currencies. The hurt for you is that you felt quietly graded, and you never quite knew what the passing mark was. The pull is their polish. Being chosen by someone that discerning felt like an award, and some part of you still wants to win it. Turn that around instead. Give one specific compliment a day: not 'nice', but 'the way you handled that call was smart'. It costs nothing, and it's the exact skill that would have changed the weather in that relationship.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin, you deserved specific praise. Asking for it plainly isn't needy.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, 'ok thumbs up' to a carefully written text is a crime in some countries.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Different currencies, real love. The exchange rate was the problem.

im-water.title: The tree that tried to schedule the ocean
im-water.text: You fell for the ocean and then tried to give it a schedule. Your Im Water ex was brilliant, restless, full of ideas that made your plans look small in a thrilling way. They watered your roots. They also disappeared for a day and then sent a three-paragraph thought at midnight, and you, who like consistent check-ins, lay awake wondering whether the silence meant something. You wanted commitment and dates on a calendar. They wanted a door open to every horizon. When you tried to channel them, they felt dammed, and when they changed direction, you felt unsafe. There was real nourishment in it, which is why it stings. They made you bigger, and you made them feel held, until held started to feel like held down. What you miss is the depth. Nobody else talks to you about the meaning of things at 2am. So check what you're actually missing. If it's the conversations, find more of them, with friends, in books, in yourself. If it's the uncertainty, be honest that you may have liked chasing the horizon more than living beside the sea.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Im, a midnight essay doesn't cancel three days of silence.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, the ocean wasn't running away. It was just being water.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Agree on a minimum, then stop policing the rest. Lesson for next time.

gye-water.title: Morning rain on the oak
gye-water.text: Your Gye Water ex cared for you the way rain cares for a tree: quietly, constantly, in ways you only noticed when it stopped. They sent songs, half-finished thoughts, a screenshot of the moon with no caption. You replied with logistics. 'Is dinner at 8?' They hinted at feelings; you asked them to just say it. When you pushed for answers, they went misty, and the harder you pushed, the further they drifted. Meanwhile they absorbed your stress without a word, until one day they were overwhelmed and you hadn't seen it coming. So here's the sting: you thought you were the strong one, and it turns out a soft person was holding you up all along. You miss that tenderness. Life with them felt nourished and seen; they noticed everything you didn't say. The practice is to answer feelings first. When a friend sends a sad song, don't ask what's wrong. Say 'that's a beautiful one, are you okay?' and wait. Soft does not mean weak. The tree learns that late, but it learns.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye, the moon screenshot was lovely. The sentence under it would've been lovelier.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, you asked 'what's wrong' like a police officer. Try 'I'm here' instead.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Rain and an oak are a good pair. They just needed subtitles.
